props.title: Snatch
props.initialSlug: Diamonds, gangsters, and boxers collide in London

sections.content: Snatch revolutionized British gangster cinema with its razor-sharp editing, intersecting plotlines, and darkly comic violence. Director Guy Ritchie built on the kinetic style he established in Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels (1998), but elevated every element - from the rapid-fire dialogue to the dizzying plot twists. Brad Pitt's deliberately unintelligible Irish Traveller boxer Mickey O'Neil became instantly iconic, while Jason Statham cemented his hardman persona as Turkish. The film's influence echoes through later British crime films like Layer Cake (2004) and RocknRolla (2008).

sections.content: The film's masterful juggling of multiple storylines - from underground boxing to diamond heists - created a template for complex crime narratives. Its influence extends beyond British cinema to Hollywood productions like Ocean's Eleven (2001) and The Italian Job (2003), which adopted similar quick-cut editing and interweaving plots. Ritchie's signature style - freeze frames, jump cuts, and witty narration - spawned countless imitators but few equals.

The casting brilliantly mixed established stars with character actors. Alan Ford's brutal Brick Top set a new standard for screen gangsters, while Benicio Del Toro's mumbling jewel thief added international appeal. The film's quotability ("Do you like dags?") and memorable characters like Boris The Blade created a new vocabulary for crime cinema that persists today. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Crime Films

Snatch created a blueprint for stylish crime comedies that balance violence with humor. Films like In Bruges (2008) and Seven Psychopaths (2012) followed this model, mixing dark comedy with criminal enterprises. The film's influence is particularly visible in British productions like Sexy Beast (2000) and Rocknrolla (2008), which maintain similar tones while telling their own distinct stories.
